articles.title: Russian sabotage attacks in Europe up 16% as Ukraine supply lines targeted, new report says
articles.summary: Russian sabotage incidents on Europe rose 16% in the year to September, with operatives using more complex explosive methods, the IISS said in a report.
articles.body: Russian sabotage incidents on Europe rose 16% in the year to September 2026, with increasingly skilled operatives using more complex explosive methods, the International Institute for Strategic Studies (IISS) said in a report. Key allies of Ukraine have accused Moscow of waging a Europe-wide campaign of drone and cyber attacks to disrupt their support for Kyiv, including an attempted drone attack at Leipzig airport in August. Moscow has rejected the accusations from ⁠Western governments and intelligence services. The IISS said that, while unskilled recruits still carried out most operations, a semi-skilled tier now used more complex methods, including improvised explosive devices with timed and remote detonators. “Arrests remove proxies but are highly unlikely to deter the RIS (Russian intelligence services) that direct them,” the London-based think tank said. The think tank said Germany and Poland would remain the most targeted states, as their transport, logistics and industrial networks were key to supplying Ukraine. In Leipzig on August 4, a drone laden with explosives was discovered near a Ukrainian Antonov cargo aircraft used for military ​supplies. Investigators suspect a second drone collided with ​a DHL cargo plane soon after the airport suspended operations. The airport is ‌a ⁠cargo and military logistics hub used by NATO and Ukraine’s Antonov Airlines for military supplies. “Targeting of critical infrastructure (specifically military-industrial and transport) accounted for more than half of recorded incidents between October 2025 and September 2026,” the IISS said. On Tuesday, Britain warned defense companies working with Ukraine’s military that they faced an increased sabotage threat from Russia. Russia’s embassy in London said at the time: “Russia has no plans, reasons or intentions to attack the U.K.” Last year, a group of British men were jailed for carrying out an arson attack on a business linked to Ukraine that British authorities had been carried out at Moscow’s behest. In September, a man was charged with providing details of a drone factory to Russian intelligence.

articles.title: TSA warns common Thanksgiving packing mistake could cause delays on the way home
articles.summary: The Transportation Security Administration notes that turkey, stuffing and pies can fly in carry-ons, but gravy and cranberry sauce must go in checked bags.
articles.body: Thanksgiving turkeys can fly in the overhead bin this holiday weekend — but the gravy will have to ride in cargo. Ahead of what could be a more than 3-million-passenger rush nationwide on the Sunday after Thanksgiving, the Transportation Security Administration (TSA) is reminding travelers about which holiday foods and drinks can clear airport checkpoints and which ones belong in checked luggage. Officials at Boston Logan International Airport, which is bracing for up to 77,000 travelers a day on Sunday and Monday, issued the reminder in an effort to keep security lines moving during the post-holiday surge. TSA WARNS TRAVELERS ABOUT SEASONAL MISTAKE THAT COULD TRIGGER AIRPORT SECURITY DELAYS The agency's rule of thumb comes down to solids versus liquids, with plenty of Thanksgiving staples falling on either side of the line. All meats — turkey, ham and chicken, for example — are considered solids and are allowed in carry-on bags. Passengers can also go through TSA with mac and cheese, stuffing, casseroles and fresh produce, including potatoes, yams, apples and cranberries. Travelers hoping to bring Thanksgiving desserts on their trip are in luck as well. TSA OFFICER SEES ALARMING SHAPES ON X-RAY BEFORE STOLEN CIVIL WAR MYSTERY UNRAVELS Holiday pies, cakes, cookies and brownies are all permitted through checkpoints, according to the TSA in a news release. But plenty of the sides and sauces that go with Thanksgiving classics will have to go in checked luggage. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The list includes cranberry sauce — both homemade and commercially canned — as well as gravy, preserves and other canned goods, as long as the items are above 3.4 ounces. "Slushy or partially melted ice packs will not be permitted through checkpoints," the TSA said. Anyone hoping to sneak prohibited items through security may have a tougher time this Thanksgiving weekend as well. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS Officials said TSA is using real-time photo ID checks, automated bin lanes and 3D scanners at Boston Logan to inspect carry-on bags while letting travelers leave electronics and small liquids packed. "Slushy or partially melted ice packs will not be permitted through checkpoints." TSA Federal Security Director for Massachusetts Bob Allison said in the press release that officers "encourage travelers to give themselves plenty of time, review what is permitted in carry-on bags and arrive at the checkpoint prepared." "These simple steps help our officers maintain strong security while keeping the passenger experience moving as efficiently as possible," added Allison. TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ Officials also encouraged Americans to check what is allowed before heading to the airport using the myTSA app or by reaching out to AskTSA online or via text message. "Additionally, travelers should ensure that any ice packs used to keep holiday foods cold are completely frozen when passing through security," TSA noted. "Slushy or partially melted ice packs will not be permitted through checkpoints." CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP Fox News Digital reached out to the TSA for additional comment.

articles.title: Trump embraced Xi, then slapped new tariffs on China: What’s his game plan?
articles.summary: US president’s new tariff regime targets China hardest, just weeks before Trump and Xi meet again in Miami.
articles.body:
In February 2025, US President Donald Trump marked his return to office by kick-starting a trade war with China.

New tariffs, amid accusations that China was failing to prevent the flow of drugs into the United States, set the stage for an escalating economic confrontation between the world’s two largest economies, which stands to reshape global trade.

While Trump’s new trade tariffs regime hit allies and rivals alike, China took the fight head-on.

Washington first put a 10 percent duty on Chinese goods, citing fentanyl and immigration concerns, and Beijing responded by curbing exports of five rare earth metals key to defence, clean energy and tech products.

Then it came to a showdown with Trump’s “ Liberation Day ” tariffs in April, including 34 percent for Chinese products. A tit-for-tat exercise ensued as headline US tariffs on China climbed to 145 percent, while US goods entering China were slapped with tariffs of 125 percent, alongside restrictions on rare earth exports.

The tariff war seesawed for much of that year before the two leaders sat at a table in October, on the sidelines of the 2025 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit in South Korea, to call a truce.

The limited-time pause in hostilities paved the way for a diplomatic thaw.

Trump then travelled to Beijing last May for talks with Xi, who then visited Washington in September for the first time in more than a decade. Trump embraced the Chinese president when he arrived in Shenzhen, China’s technology hub, earlier this month for this year’s APEC summit.

But then Trump returned to Washington and, in less than a week, his administration had announced a new tariff regime – its second attempt at reshaping its trade war after the Supreme Court declared his Liberation Day tariffs of April last year illegal.

“The practical purpose is simple: rebuild [the] tariff leverage the Supreme Court stripped away and force Beijing to the table before the next summit,” said Alicia Garcia-Herrero, the chief economist for Asia Pacific at investment bank Natixis.

This time, the Trump administration has announced plans to impose new tariffs on 14 of its major trading partners, including China, the European Union and India, accusing them of flooding world markets with cheap goods through unfair government subsidies, policies and suppressed wages.

China is subject to the highest rates – a new 20 percent levy that is still within the bounds of the trade truce that is set to expire in January. Washington has, however, threatened a 40 percent levy if trade talks break down .

Instead of the emergency powers it used the first time – and which the Supreme Court struck down – the Trump administration is using Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974, alleging that targeted countries are making use of “structural excess capacity”. It has identified these 14 specific economies during an investigation it launched in March, but views China as the biggest offender, particularly in its steel, aluminium, electric cars, household appliances and solar panels industries.

Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Hinrich Foundation, a trade policy think tank in Singapore, said the “original intention” of the investigation “was to provide a more durable way to get back to the tariff levels” announced on Liberation Day.

“Over that time, I think the purpose changed somewhat,” she told Al Jazeera.

“Originally a means to apply tariffs, it seems clear that the White House wants a more sweeping use of Section 301, which allows a broad range of activities to be subject to possible negotiations and future punishment like tariffs,” she added.

Elms argued that Trump’s announcement coming in “now is rather interesting”, given he is due to meet with Xi next month, in Miami, at the G20 Leaders’ Summit. “This announcement adds another layer of possible tensions,” she said.

Just before Trump landed in Shenzhen, where he was greeted by Xi on the tarmac, earlier this month, the Chinese leader had opened the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) leaders’ meeting with a call to “reduce barriers to trade and investment”.

Xi also portrayed Beijing as a stable trade partner in contrast with the US, where Trump’s tariff war had already rattled global economic equations.

Responding to the latest round of tariffs this week, Beijing warned that it “reserves the right” to retaliate with steeper tariffs.

“China urges the US to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” a Ministry of Commerce spokesperson said, adding that Beijing “will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests”.

Referring to the eight-month investigation into “structural excess capacity” practices undertaken by Jamieson Greer, Trump’s trade representative, China said it was “a typical act of unilateralism that severely disrupts the international economic order and seriously violates WTO rules”.

Under the latest measures, Washington is seeking to take its economic confrontation with Beijing beyond bilateral trade, targeting the industrial policies of countries emerging as alternative manufacturing hubs but whose supply chains remain closely intertwined with China’s.

Hinrich Foundation’s Elms told Al Jazeera that while Beijing “is probably ok with a 20 percent tariff, they are undoubtedly less comfortable with the attempt to hold all other trade partners accountable to the US for engagement with China”.

Investment bank Natixis’s Herrero said that Trump’s latest tariffs “are less a grand strategy than a familiar negotiating ploy: keep the pressure on after a friendly photo-op”, referring to the meeting in Shenzhen.

“The stated rationale is Chinese overcapacity,” she said, adding that, however, the aim is to “rebuild tariff leverage” and “force Beijing to the table before the next summit”.

Chen Bo, a senior research fellow at the National University of Singapore (NUS), said the new measures are a substitute for the struck-down reciprocal tariffs, with “the same kind of inherent reasons or motivations”.

Bo argued that the US government “needs to raise money to keep its many activities going, including the war on Iran”. Furthermore, “it cannot rely on the bond market due to high interest rates – and consumer inflation already hit them hard in midterm election results”.

“Tariff money is one of the easiest ways to finance itself, rather than asking for more from Congress,” Bo told Al Jazeera.

Despite nearly a decade of the ongoing trade tensions between the US and China, Beijing’s global goods trade surplus reached a record $1.19 trillion last year, underscoring the scale of its export dominance. By comparison, the US ran a $1.24 trillion goods trade deficit over the same period.

“Nothing has changed substantially over the years,” he said, adding that “no new tariff will be effective to reduce the Chinese overcapacity at all, or in a significant way.”

Bo said he believes both China and the US are “working hard on the trade negotiations to de-escalate or mitigate” before the two leaders meet again next month, where they want to discuss issues like AI, nuclear weapons and the wars in Iran and Ukraine. “That’s a much bigger picture for them than a trade relationship,” Bo said.

For Beijing’s part, Herrero said that “China can still blunt” these new measures by the US.

“Rare earths remain its sharpest tool,” she added.

“The risk for Trump is the same as always: higher prices land on American consumers, and the wider trade system frays further,” Herrero said. “Whether that counts as a feature or a bug depends on how much pain Washington is willing to absorb.”

articles.title: Police officers discovered Chloe Mitchell's remains in bins, court hears
articles.summary: The jury was previously told Brandon Rainey accepted he had killed Chloe but would rely on the partial defence of diminished responsibility.
articles.body:
Police and forensics officers have told a court how they discovered the dismembered remains of Chloe Mitchell in bins.

Brandon Rainey, formerly of James Street in Ballymena, is on trial accused of murdering Chloe and preventing the lawful burial of her remains, which he denies.

The 21-year-old's body parts were found in wheelie bins near Rainey's flat in Ballymena on 11 June 2023, eight days after the prosecution says she was murdered by the defendant in his home.

The jury was previously told Rainey, 30, accepted he had killed Chloe but would rely on the partial defence of diminished responsibility.

A police officer told Belfast Crown Court on Friday that when he was carrying out house-to-house enquiries in James Street, a resident apologised for a smell coming from her bin.

The officer said as he and a constable walked across an alleyway he noticed a very strong smell and went back to the resident's home and looked in her bin.

He said when he opened the bin it was "full to the brim" and there were maggots and a bad smell which left him struggling not to vomit.

The officer said he then came across another bin which had flies coming out of it.

A crime scene investigator recounted to the court how she had searched two of the bins and found body parts inside them in black bin liners.

Her evidence was followed by evidence from another crime scene investigator who examined the inside of Rainey's flat on 8 June, the day Rainey was arrested.

He told the court he had seized a number of items including a duvet, protein container and tracksuit bottoms which were all stained with suspected blood, as well as a knife in a sheath.

The following day he returned and seized more items including black bags and a roll of masking tape.

Blood stains matched Chloe's DNA profile

His evidence was followed by a forensic scientist who is an expert in body fluids, blood pattern analysis and DNA profiling.

He told the court he found blood stains in and outside the property, most of which matched Chloe's DNA profile.

Under cross-examination from defence barrister Des Fahy KC, the forensic scientist confirmed the work he carried out could not determine when the blood or DNA he examined was deposited.

He also said it was the case that his work could not assist in terms of the exact circumstances in which the blood or DNA were deposited.

Earlier on Friday, the jury of seven men and five women heard the latest sections of transcripts of Rainey's police interviews.

Rainey told detectives he had never been "physical or violent" towards Chloe, adding: "I don't do that to a woman."

When police asked him if she ever talked about anyone threatening her, Rainey said his younger brother Cameron had attacked Chloe.

He said Chloe, who was Cameron's cousin, had tried to pick him up when he was "paralytic drunk" and he had gone "into a mad rage", thrown Chloe into a kerb and knocked her front teeth out.

Rainey also told detectives they were "gaslighting" him by asking him "too many questions" and said it was "like a manipulation technique".

articles.title: Sharad Pawar's NCP backs Centre's delimitation Bill ahead of Special Session
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: NCP (SP) on Friday supported the Centre's proposed delimitation Bill, which is set to be tabled during the special session of Parliament.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: NCP (SP) on Friday supported the Centre's proposed delimitation Bill, which is set to be tabled during the special session of Parliament.NCP (SP) leader Jitendra Awhad said that a consensus was reached after discussions with Sharad Pawar, adding that the delimitation process is a constitutional requirement."The discussion wasn't about our party's official stance. The general point being made was that the delimitation process is a constitutional requirement," Awhad said."A decision has been made to support the delimitation process, and we will indeed support it. We will support the delimitation," he addedMeanwhile Shirur MP Amol Kolhe, the party's whip in the Lok Sabha, said any decision would be taken only after studying the bill."Sule had made the party's stand clear. We have to first study the draft of the bill, only then any decision can be taken," he said.This comes after the party's national working president Supriya Sule, on Thursday, struck a softer tone on the Centre's proposal, saying it would be premature to oppose the legislation before its details were known."Let the bill come. Perhaps there could be something good in the Delimitation Bill," she told news agency PTI."Whether a bill is in the country's interest or not, opposing it just because you are in the opposition, or blindly supporting it because you are in power, is wrong for a healthy democracy. It is not necessary to oppose everything. We can also suggest improvements and say what changes should be made. There could be something good in it," Sule said.Earlier in the day, Sule said that she would not attend the INDIA bloc meeting scheduled for Saturday to discuss the Opposition's floor strategy for the special Parliament session, as her father Sharad Pawar was ailing."I will go to Delhi on Monday morning to attend the session," she said in her WhatsApp status message.The NCP (SP) also issued a whip directing its Lok Sabha MPs to remain present in the House from November 30.The NCP (SP), which has eight Lok Sabha MPs, took this stand amid discussions on the numbers needed to pass a constitutional amendment linked to delimitation.Such legislation requires a special two-thirds majority of members present and voting.Factoring in five current vacancies in the 543-member House, the effective strength stands at 538, putting the two-thirds threshold at approximately 359 votes.Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.title: Eisenkot navigates tricky waters as he tests power-sharing with Netanyahu
articles.summary: Some of his allies are calling for such an arrangement, but it would represent a betrayal of his pre-election promise.
articles.body:
The 2026 Israeli elections were termed the most consequential in recent decades for the country – for multiple reasons.

For Benjamin Netanyahu, the caretaker prime minister, and his right-wing coalition, the elections were about keeping the far-right in power to protect the formative changes they enacted in state policies and institutions. For the anti-Netanyahu bloc led by Gadi Eisenkot – or the “change bloc”, as it is referred to – the promise was to replace the failed October 7 government as they termed it, rehabilitate Israel’s international standing, and end internal divisions.

Once the results were announced, things changed. Gadi Eisenkot was tasked with forming Israel’s next government. But his bloc does not have enough seats in the Knesset to win a vote of confidence on its own. The United Arab List and the Joint List, parties led by Palestinian citizens of Israel, have 19 seats and are willing to back Eisenkot in his efforts to replace Netanyahu as Israel’s premier. But some in the change bloc, such as Avigdor Lieberman , promised not to support any government coalition that includes an Arab-led party or one that depended on votes from Palestinian citizens of Israel.

This, despite the fact that Lieberman himself became chair of the Knesset’s Foreign Affairs and Defense Committee thanks to those same votes. That contradiction was pointed out by Mohamed Majadli, the chief editor of AlNas Radio in Israel and an analyst on the country’s Channel 12.

In such a limited space for political manoeuvres, Eisenkot embarked on forming a coalition, holding talks with his partners, while also trying to open channels of communication with ultra-Orthodox parties, particularly the United Torah Judaism party. At the same time, former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett led efforts to form a unity government with Netanyahu’s Likud party and succeeded in convincing Eisenkot’s Yashar party to open formal talks with Likud.

The prospect of reneging on the change bloc’s central promise to oust Netanyahu looms large over these talks. Bennett and others are advocating for that outcome in light of the lack of a clear Zionist majority against Israel’s longest-serving prime minister.

Meanwhile, leader of the Democrats group, Yair Golan, has publicly opposed any unity formula with Netanyahu and has called out Bennett for his efforts to reach it. The Yashar-Likud talks are complex and overshadowed by, among other issues, accusations between the two sides.

Netanyahu accuses the change bloc of working to undermine Israel by working with Arab-led parties, which he has referred to as “the enemy”. Eisenkot has gone on the record saying that Netanyahu endangers the security of Israel and is willing to ignite war for his personal gain.

From Likud’s perspective, a unity government would require a rotation agreement on the premiership. That means that rather than getting rid of Netanyahu, Eisenkot would have to agree to Netanyahu staying on as prime minister for two years, or agreeing to serve second in the rotation.

This scenario gained traction after judges presiding over Netanyahu corruption trials recommended dropping the most serious charge of bribery, as well as reconsidering the charges or reaching a plea bargain in the others. This development has strengthened Netanyahu’s negotiating position and prompted him to call for an end to the political boycott against him.

Against this backdrop, Eisenkot is manoeuvring through dangerous political waters. If he fails to form a government, voters may be forced to return to the polls again while Netanyahu remains at the helm. This scenario could translate into a loss of support for the change bloc and hand Netanyahu a renewed mandate, while simultaneously ending the political careers of some leaders such as Eisenkot.

If Eisenkot chooses unity with Netanyahu over the promises he made to his voters, he will lose credibility among supporters. Additionally, Eisenkot could be outmanoeuvred by Netanyahu.

Many point to the coalition agreement between Benjamin Netanyahu and Benny Gantz in 2020, which included a rotating premiership. The government collapsed before Benny Gantz assumed his position and his political career never recovered.

In political terms, forming a unity government with Netanyahu would represent a reversal of election promises on fundamental issues such as transparency, judicial reform, and the influence of religion on the state, because unlike the change bloc, Netanyahu’s allies are already embedded in the state bureaucracy and able to entrench these policies.

More strategically, it reflects the knee-jerk reaction of Israel’s body politic to Palestinian citizens of Israel. This is what leading sociologist and researcher Honaida Ghanem calls Israel’s structural problem: its inability to reconcile that part of Israel’s political and leadership crisis is that in today’s Israel, anti-Arab sentiment is one of the few policies most Jewish Israelis can agree on, while they no longer agree on the nature of the state, the influence of religion over the state, or many other fundamental issues of identity and governance.

The prospect of a unity government with Eisenkot and Netanyahu remains possible, though not likely, primarily because of the personal and political risks such an unholy political marriage would entail for the change bloc leaders.

articles.title: Treasure hunters searching a field uncover 5,500-coin hoard hiding 'national treasure'
articles.summary: Archaeologist Anne Skogsfjord spotted the rare Saint Olaf coin inside Norway's largest Viking Age hoard, the first such find there since 1924, officials said.
articles.body: Archaeologists in Norway have uncovered an extraordinarily rare 1,000-year-old coin minted during the reign of Viking King Olaf Haraldsson, better known as Saint Olaf, inside the largest Viking Age coin hoard ever found in the country. The discovery, announced by the Museum of Cultural History in Oslo, marks the first time a coin of this type has been found in Norway since 1924. The Olaf coin went on display Nov. 20 at the Historical Museum in Oslo — part of the University of Oslo's Museum of Cultural History — as part of a new exhibition showcasing the Mørstad Hoard. PUZZLING SOUND IN BACKYARD LEADS HOMEOWNER TO MASSIVE 1,000-YEAR-OLD TREASURE The hoard was originally discovered on April 10 by metal detectorists Vegard Sørlie and Rune Sætre in Rena, Innlandet County, and the site has since been secured and investigated for further research. Officials said the latest count puts the cache at 5,500 coins, though researchers believe the total could soon exceed 6,000. The star of the hoard, officials said, is a coin depicting Haraldsson, who ruled from 1015 to 1028. Haraldsson, who became a saint after his death, occupies "a unique place in Norwegian history," officials said. RARE COIN BEARING FACE OF KING WITH INFAMOUS NICKNAME UNEARTHED AFTER 1,000 YEARS "Fewer than 20 of his coins have survived to the present day, and most have been found outside Norway," the release said. "Only four examples of the type found in the Mørstad Hoard have previously been discovered, including just one in Norway." The new coin was spotted by archaeologist Anne Skogsfjord, who immediately ran to tell a colleague about the find. Officials said the coin was initially thought to be Anglo-Saxon and had been roughly sorted into the group of coins issued by Æthelred II. MYSTERIOUS FIND BENEATH FIELD LEADS MAN TO MASSIVE TREASURE HIDDEN FOR CENTURIES "I could see that it read ONLAF R+ NORMANORV … Could this really be a coin of Olaf Haraldsson that I was holding?" Skogsfjord said. "And it was! It was a very special moment." She added, "I realized that we had found a national treasure." "When you think this Viking treasure cannot become any more exciting, new surprises emerge." The coin dates between 1024 and 1028, and officials said it may have been in circulation for up to 25 years before it was deposited in the hoard. Featuring a cross on both sides, the coin shows how Olaf used currency to legitimize the Christian faith and establish himself as a Christian king of European standing, according to numismatics expert Svein H. Gullbekk. CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER The museum added, "Few archaeological and historical sources can be directly linked to Olaf Haraldsson himself. Numismatic sources — the coins — were closely connected to the king." Gullbekk said in the release, "Olaf Haraldsson himself decided what these coins should look like, and perhaps he was present when they were struck. It is entirely possible that this very coin from Mørstad was once held in the king's own hand." Hanna Geiran, Norway's director general of cultural heritage, said the coin "is not only a rare object, but also tangible testimony from a time when the foundations of the Norwegian kingdom and the Christianization of the country were laid." "When you think this Viking treasure cannot become any more exciting, new surprises emerge," said Geiran, the museum noted. CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS "This St. Olaf coin is yet another reminder of how extraordinary this find is." Looking ahead, the museum said that research on the coin hoard will continue "for a long time to come." "Every single coin must undergo the same thorough process before entering the museum collection," added officials. "Numismatists, archaeologists, conservators, collection managers and photographers are all involved." TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ The Mørstad Hoard joins several other significant European coin discoveries unearthed in recent months. Earlier this year, archaeologists in Germany uncovered 11 ancient Celtic coins at a construction site — the largest hoard of its kind ever found in the region, dating back more than 2,000 years. articles.title: Birders flock to Blyth retail park to see waxwings
articles.summary: About 30 of the birds have been spotted feasting on berries at Albion Retail Park in Blyth.
articles.body:
Birdwatchers have been gathering at a retail park to see a flock of birds which do not breed in the UK.

Waxwings are most commonly found in the forests of Scandinavia and Western Russia and migrate to the UK in the winter in search of berries, their favourite food.

But a flock of about 30 has been spotted at the Albion Retail Park in Blyth, Northumberland, this week, with birders travelling miles to catch a glimpse.

"There are a lot of people who travel a distance to come and see these birds," Blyth birder Wayne Eastlake said. "If they're there regularly, it's going to be worth the journey."

He credits waxwings with sparking his interest in birds and photography when he was 10 years old.

Now 73, Eastlake said it was fantastic to see the birds in his hometown.

Waxwings have a peachy-buff coloured body and a sleek crest and their migration patterns are "unpredictable", according to the RSPB.

Birder Colin Bradshaw predicted hundreds of waxwings would be spotted in the country this winter as some berry crops had failed in Scandinavia.

"In most years we would see one or two in a winter in Northumberland," he said.

"But this year we've had up to about 15 in Alnwick already, there are about 10 in Hexham, there have been over 30 in Blyth.

"This year looks like it's going to be one of the big waxwing years."

Bradshaw said birdwatchers were excited to have a good chance of seeing the starling-sized birds.

"It means that instead of having to go long distances and stand around for ages hoping to see one, you can go and see your local flock."

He said waxwings were attracted to trees and bushes with lots of berries, such as the rowan, hawthorn and cotoneaster planted on housing estates built between the 1960s and 1980s - which could give residents a surprise.

"If you're one of those people who has a tree or bush with lots of berries in your garden, you can wake up one morning and find you've got 30 cameras trained on your window," Bradshaw said.

Eastlake called on birders to be respectful when trying to get shots of the waxwings and said they did not need to go so close to them.

"They've [cameras] all got telephoto lenses so you don't need to be sitting on top of them," he said.

"Even on modern iPhones you can zoom in and get a half-decent picture."

Both have been keen to share their experience of seeing waxwings with the general public.

"People in Blyth are fascinated and they're delighted people are coming to their town to see them," Bradshaw said.

"And most birdwatchers are keen to show people."

articles.title: Why is Israel celebrating Costa Rica’s ban on Francesca Albanese?
articles.summary: Costa Rica is under pressure over its decision to bar the UN expert who has documented Israel’s genocidal war on Gaza.
articles.body:
Costa Rica has banned United Nations independent rapporteur Francesca Albanese from entering the country over what officials described as the risk she poses to national security.

Albanese has been one of Israel’s foremost critics, documenting its genocidal war on Gaza as well as its systematic discrimination against Palestinians and illegal settlement in occupied Palestinian territory since 1967.

Albanese was stopped by police on security grounds on Thursday as she arrived at Juan Santamaria international airport in the capital San Jose, where she was due to be presented with an honorary degree from the University of Costa Rica.

Albanese, who called the move “a disgrace”, was still being held at the airport on Friday.

Omer Badilla, the director-general of Costa Rica’s immigration authority, later appeared to offer some explanation on social media, saying Albanese “was refused entry to the country because she is the subject of an international alert due to links to terrorist acts”, without specifying the nature of that alert or which country had issued it.

“It is important to note that when national security is at risk, as is the case here, our police authorities strictly enforce the provisions of our legal system,” Badilla said.

While the move was welcomed by Israel, including by its Ambassador to the UN, Danny Danon, a number of Costa Rican and regional figures and rights groups, as well as the University of Costa Rica, have objected to the treatment of Albanese and demanded an explanation.

On Thursday, the Association of Human Rights Lawyers, Judges and Prosecutors of Latin America and the Caribbean (AJUFIDH) urged the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights to seek answers from the Costa Rican government, arguing that the ban may violate international obligations protecting UN experts.

Costa Rican lawmakers from several political parties have also criticised the move, describing it as arbitrary and damaging to the country’s reputation for defending human rights and international law, while the University of Costa Rica has formally requested that immigration authorities and foreign ministry officials explain the legal grounds for the decision.

Why would Israel celebrate a UN figure not being allowed entry to Costa Rica?

As Special Rapporteur, Albanese has used her position to document Israeli violations of international law. She accuses Israel of committing genocide in Gaza, maintaining an apartheid system against Palestinians and pursuing territorial expansion through illegal settlements in occupied East Jerusalem and the West Bank.

In her March 2024 report, Anatomy of a Genocide , for which she received numerous threats , Albanese found that there were reasonable grounds to conclude that Israel had committed acts prohibited under the UN Genocide Convention. She subsequently called for an arms embargo, sanctions against Israel and an end to the trade and financial relationships sustaining its occupation.

Throughout her tenure, Albanese has repeatedly described the occupation of Palestinian territory as an entrenched system of apartheid and settler colonialism, arguing that the displacement of Palestinians and expansion of illegal Israeli settlements are part of a much wider process of territorial dispossession.

She has also challenged Israel’s international backers, accusing governments of providing diplomatic protection and military assistance while failing to uphold their obligations under international law.

In her July 2025 report , she went further still, naming companies including Microsoft, Amazon and Google , alongside arms manufacturers and financial institutions, which she said were helping to sustain Israel’s occupation and military campaign. She called on governments to sever trade and financial ties with Israel, impose an arms embargo and hold companies accountable.

On Friday, Balkees Jarrah, Middle East and North Africa director at Human Rights Watch, told Al Jazeera: “The Costa Rican authorities’ decision to bar Francesca Albanese entry comes in the context of increasing efforts aimed at muzzling criticism of Israeli authorities’ atrocity crimes against Palestinians, ensuring impunity for these abuses, and other governments’ complicity in them.”

Born to a lawyer and a homemaker in a small town in the Campania region of southern Italy in 1977, Albanese has said her interest in Israeli-Palestinian politics was shaped by her father’s library, where she encountered the writings of Holocaust survivor Primo Levi. She was also inspired by her older brother’s bedroom posters supporting Palestine during the first Intifada.

After studying law at the University of Pisa and human rights at SOAS in London, she pursued a career with the UN, first in Africa, then in Geneva and finally in Jerusalem with UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees, before going on to be appointed Special Rapporteur on human rights in the occupied Palestinian territories in May 2022.

Is this the first time Israel and its allies have targeted Albanese?

Israel and its supporters have been campaigning against Albanese for years, repeatedly accusing her of anti-Semitism and anti-Israel bias and calling for her removal from her UN post.

The campaign intensified in 2023, when Israel and pro-Israel organisations stepped up demands for her dismissal following allegations that some of her public comments crossed the line into anti-Semitism.

In January that year, 11 US members of Congress signed a bipartisan letter urging the UN to remove her, while Israeli government officials also called for her resignation. Albanese rejected the accusations, saying they were intended to discredit her work documenting Israeli abuses.

The most significant escalation came in July 2025, when the Trump administration imposed sanctions against Albanese, accusing her of pursuing a campaign of political and economic warfare against Israel and the United States.

The measures included restrictions on Albanese entering the US, blocking her property and financial interests subject to US jurisdiction and prohibiting US nationals from engaging in transactions with her, effectively isolating her from much of the US financial system.

The US decision was roundly condemned by the UN and various rights groups.

A committee of the UN’s Human Rights Council characterised it as just one aspect of the “continued assault of the current US administration on the entire UN system and its core values of human rights, justice, accountability and the rule of law”. Rights groups, including Human Rights Watch (HRW) and Amnesty International, also criticised the decision, with the latter slamming the US measures as a “disgraceful affront to international justice”.

articles.title: What’s behind Trump’s post about Iraq?
articles.summary: US President Donald Trump on Friday backed Iraq’s efforts to assert control over its oil resources and arms, a move that cements Washington’s alignment with Baghdad as it juggles a showdown with the Kurdish region and the country’s Iran-backed militants.
articles.body: US President Donald Trump on Friday backed Iraq’s efforts to assert control over its oil resources and arms, a move that cements Washington’s alignment with Baghdad as it juggles a showdown with the Kurdish region and the country’s Iran-backed militants. “We support Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi’s efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state,” Trump said Friday on Truth Social. “We support Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s efforts to build a united, prosperous, and strong Iraq that makes its own political decisions,” he wrote. A 41-year-old Iraqi businessman, al-Zaidi assumed power in May amid the US-Iran war. He immediately launched an aggressive anti-corruption campaign that sought to consolidate both the country’s oil and arms under state control at a time when Iran-backed militias were firing at US interests. The Iraqi leader is supported by US Special Envoy for Iraq, Tom Barrack, who is close to Trump and considered to be influential in regional US policy. “Al-Zaidi has forged a very, very strong relationship with Tom Barrack, who has the president’s ear,” Hamdi Malik, an associate fellow at The Washington Institute think tank and founder of Iraq Monitor, told CNN. In June, al-Zaidi “reaffirmed Iraq’s commitment to deepening trade and investment relations” between Iraq and the US, and to allowing US oil companies to resume operations “with full security guarantees,” according to a joint statement. A month later Trump welcomed al-Zaidi at the White House, where he called him “a great fighter” and “a great fan of America.” Trump’s post comes amid escalating tensions with the semi-autonomous Kurdistan Region of Iraq. On Friday, state media reported that Iraq had declared that the export of crude outside the state oil company SOMO will be considered “smuggling” as revenues do not enter the state treasury. Iraqi authorities estimate that oil exported from the Kurdistan Region led to a revenue loss of more than $100 billion between 2008 and 2025 for Baghdad, Iraqi government spokesman Haider al-Aboudi said. The Kurdistan Region, also known as Iraqi Kurdistan, is rich in oil. It has long aspired to self-determination and has for years been caught in disputes with Baghdad over oil and trade. On Thursday, Baghdad ordered the closure of all “unofficial” border crossings, including those with Syria and Iran, that were administered by the Kurdistan Region’s government. Tensions further escalated between Baghdad and Iraqi Kurdistan after demonstrations broke out Thursday over what Kurdish leaders view as an infringement of the region’s rights by Baghdad. In a rare joint statement, the Kurdish Region’s two competing parties protested Baghdad’s decision to take over oil fields and border crossings, calling it “a red line,” the Erbil-based Kurdish broadcaster Rudaw said. Trump’s post also delivered a blow to Iraq’s Iran-backed militants, who have yet to place their weapons under state control. State forces and the heavily armed Kataib Hezbollah militant group clashed last week after Iraqi forces deployed to the group’s stronghold town of Jurf al-Sakhar – one of Prime Minister al-Zaidi’s focal points in his sweeping anti-corruption campaign. Trump’s post is an unusual way of doing politics, Malik said, where the US makes its position “clear” to the Iraqis and the Kurds.

articles.title: Hackers attack and penetrate Air Force’s computing platform
articles.summary: Hackers penetrated the Air Force’s cloud computing platform in a breach that could have exposed sensitive military information, a U.S. official said Friday.
articles.body: Hackers penetrated the Air Force’s cloud computing platform in a breach that could have exposed sensitive military information, a U.S. official said Friday. The official confirmed the hack to NBC News but could not provide any additional information about timing or the attack’s impact. “The department of the Air Force does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems,” an Air Force spokesperson said. Reuters first reported about this most recent cyberintrusion against federal assets. The FBI’s National Crime Information Center — which is used by federal, state and local authorities to share important information — was recently breached, sources briefed on the matter told NBC News this week. And about two months ago, the FBI and Dutch national police arrested leaders of a “global cybercrime and threat actor group” that allegedly stole employee information from a bureau database. It is unclear whether any of these breaches are related. “We continuously take prudent measures to protect department information, systems, and mission capabilities,” the Air Force spokesperson said Friday. “Ensuring the security, resilience, and availability of our most critical war fighting assets remains a top priority.” “The department continues to assess and modernize its enterprise cloud capabilities to meet, evolving mission, security, resilience, and user requirements,” the statement continued. “Decisions regarding technical architecture, workload placement, contracts, and future capabilities are made through established governance, acquisition, and risk management processes.” This is a developing story. articles.title: Australian police hunt ‘absolute jerk’ who attacked iconic ancient tree with chainsaw
articles.summary: Police in Western Australia are looking for the “absolute jerk” who took a chainsaw to a centuries-old tree in a “senseless” act of vandalism, local politicians have said.
articles.body: Police in Western Australia are looking for the “absolute jerk” who took a chainsaw to a centuries-old tree in a “senseless” act of vandalism, local politicians have said. King Jarrah, which is believed to be between 300 to 500 years old, surviving bush fires and storms, is one of the largest jarrah trees in Wellington National Park, south of Perth, standing at 36 meters tall, or 118 feet, according to the park. The reserve put out an alert on Tuesday that it would be closing its King Jarrah site and parking lot “due to safety concerns after a tree was vandalised,” and that the area would “remain closed until deemed safe for visitors.” “In an act that I can only describe as appalling, senseless, and heartbreaking, some absolute jerk has seen fit to vandalise the Wellington National Park’s iconic King Jarrah Tree with a chainsaw!” Matthew Swinbourn, minister for the environment of Western Australia, said Thursday in a joint post on Facebook with Jodie Hanns, parliamentary secretary to the minister for energy and decarbonisation. “It’s hard to fathom how shocking it is that someone would do this to a tree believed to be about 500 years old, particularly in a national park,” the statement continues. “Western Australians love this tree. Our community will be heartbroken, and they have every right to be angry,” the statement adds. Experts are assessing the tree’s condition, “but right now our focus is on giving it every possible chance of survival and finding those responsible,” the politicians said. “Whoever did this has damaged something precious to all of us,” they added. Surveillance cameras have been installed in the area, and the site remains closed, Swinbourn and Hanns said, urging people not to visit the site. They called on anyone who knows anything to “come forward. Anyone capable of such a deliberate and callous act should be held accountable.” Tree might have to ‘come down’ Police officers say the incident occurred between Saturday and Sunday, and a silver Jeep was subsequently seen in the area, the Australian Broadcasting Corporation reported Friday. They said the car’s occupants may be able to assist with inquiries. Peter Murphy, convenor of local conservation organization Preston Environment Group, told the public broadcaster that the incident made his “heart sink,” adding: “Looking at the damage on scene photographs … I fear it may have to actually come down.” In a statement Friday, councillor Tyrrell Gardiner, president of the Shire of Dardanup local government, joined calls for those responsible to “be identified,” and expressed hope that the tree would survive. “The King Jarrah is one of the most recognised natural landmarks on our doorstep and something many Dardanup residents have grown up visiting with family and friends,” he said. “To see it deliberately damaged is distressing and unacceptable,” Gardiner added. “We hope the King Jarrah can recover from this damage and continue to stand as a symbol of the natural heritage that makes our region so special.”

articles.title: Putin’s biggest ally questions a key claim Russia uses to justify invasion of Ukraine
articles.summary: Russia’s closest ally Belarus has questioned the logic behind Moscow’s claim over Ukrainian territory, likening it to Mongolia demanding to take over Russian lands.
articles.body: Russia’s closest ally Belarus has questioned the logic behind Moscow’s claim over Ukrainian territory, likening it to Mongolia demanding to take over Russian lands. Russian President Vladimir Putin has argued that Ukraine should be part of Russia because Kyiv was at the heart of the medieval federation known as the Ancient Rus. Experts have long said this was – at best – an exercise in historical revisionism, but now even Belarusian President Alexander Lukashenko, who is usually hand in hand with Putin, has cast doubt on the claim. Lukashenko told French magazine Le Point in an interview published Wednesday that, “to say that (Ukraine’s) lands were Russian from ancient times … well, Russian lands, if you look deeper, were once Mongol-Tatar. Remember? So then, according to that logic, all of Russia should be given to whom – Mongolia?” In the wide-ranging interview laced with falsehoods and inaccuracies that was otherwise largely supportive of Russia, Lukashenko told the magazine he believed Putin understood the logic was flawed, calling him a “shrewd, clever politician.” Speaking to the French magazine, Lukashenko celebrated his friendship with Putin and repeated the Russian leader’s false narratives about Ukraine starting the war by “killing and burning Russian people.” Lukashenko’s convictions, and close relationship with Putin, go back a long time. He was the only member of the Belarusian parliament who voted against the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. And, during his 32 years as president, he has effectively turned Belarus into Russia’s vassal state. Under his watch, Belarus has played a key role in the war in Ukraine. In February 2022, Lukashenko allowed Russia to use Belarus as a launching pad for Moscow’s full-scale invasion – even though he now denies knowing about it. Later, he agreed to host Russian tactical nuclear weapons. “Putin and I can joke together, and we are all on informal, first-name terms with one another. He’s entirely approachable,” Lukashenko said, contrasting his relationship with Putin to that of US President Donald Trump’s relationship with the leaders of Western countries. “You would never say such things to Trump. You sat around that table in Washington like parrots, afraid to say anything to him, sorry for putting it this way. He said whatever he wanted, even in a mocking manner. That is simply unacceptable among us,” he said. Zelensky rejects Lukashenko offer Lukashenko also suggested he would be open to taking Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky to see Putin. “I could board a plane together and fly to Moscow. The two of us. As the guarantor of his security, I could sit down with him and fly to Moscow,” he said. Addressing that suggestion, Zelensky dismissed it as “not serious.” “We are at war, we cannot meet in Moscow, we cannot meet in Kyiv. We all understand this perfectly well. When someone says such things, it is simply not a serious conversation,” he said. Lukashenko also said he believed Russia would eventually take over the entire eastern Ukrainian Donbas region, but he pushed back on some of Putin’s maximalist demands – such as the return of NATO’s borders to where they were in 1997. “I am absolutely convinced that this is the start of negotiations. In any negotiations, both sides proceed from certain maximum conditions. But in the process of negotiations, one must sit at the table and negotiate,” Lukashenko told the publication.

articles.title: Body found in woodland near Springholm confirmed as Kelsey Hunter
articles.summary: Kelsey Hunter's body was found in a wooded area near the village of Springholm where she lived.
articles.body:
Police have confirmed that a body found in woodland in southern Scotland has been identified as missing 20-year-old Kelsey Hunter.

She had last been seen in Castle Douglas at 17:00 on Saturday and a major search was carried out around the nearby village of Springholm where she lived.

On Tuesday, Daniel McKnight, 21, appeared on petition at Dumfries Sheriff Court charged with murder and two other charges, including defeating the ends of justice. Kelsey's body was found at about 19:15 on Wednesday.

McKnight made no plea and was remanded in custody.

The search operation around the Dumfries and Galloway village concluded when the body was found but police said extensive inquiries remained ongoing with a number of resources being used - including forensic specialists.

Det Ch Insp Stephen McGrath said: "Our thoughts remain with Kelsey's family at this incredibly difficult time, and we are continuing to provide them with support.

"They have asked that their privacy is respected.

"Extensive work remains ongoing and a team of officers are continuing to carry out inquiries."

He thanked everyone who had come forward with information so far and said officers would remain in the area while the investigation continued.

Door-to-door and CCTV inquiries are still being carried out.

Local area commander Emma Dodds said: "We understand how upsetting this has been for the local community, but we continue to have a significant amount of resources dedicated to this investigation.

He asked anyone with any concerns, or information to contact police .

A large police presence has been in the village - which sits next to the A75 that runs from Gretna to Stranraer - since Sunday evening.

Dogs, a helicopter and specialist officers were involved in the search while officers made door-to-door inquiries.

Dumfries and Galloway Council has been offering support to the village primary which is close to where a police cordon was in place.

It said a message had been sent to the community to reassure them that the school continued to be a "safe and nurturing space".

The local authority's principal education psychologist has also been working with the primary and Castle Douglas High School to "provide support to learners and staff".

articles.title: Former Ashfield District Council leader jailed for fraud and tax evasion
articles.summary: Jason Zadrozny sobs in the dock as he is sentenced to 27 months in prison.
articles.body:
A former council leader accused of inventing a fake heritage society to scam a local authority out of thousands of pounds has been jailed for 27 months.

Jason Zadrozny set up the Ashfield Heritage Society before applying for council funding, which he then transferred into his personal account.

He claimed the cash was "to support heritage projects", but pocketed the money for himself. He was convicted of fraud and tax evasion on 21 September following a trial.

At Northampton Crown Court on Friday, the 46-year-old, of Stanton Hill, sobbed in the dock as Judge David Herbert KC told him he had "failed the electorate and harmed public confidence in the district council by your fraudulent conduct".

The six-week trial heard Ashfield District Council leader and county councillor Zadrozny - of the Ashfield Independents - set up the heritage society in 2018 before applying for funding from Nottinghamshire County Council.

This, the trial heard, included £7,500, requested three days after setting up a bank account for the society, which Zadrozny claimed was "to support heritage projects in Ashfield".

The council issued the funds and they were sent directly to Zadrozny, who deposited them in the account, before withdrawing them in cash in March.

Prosecutors alleged part of the money was used to buy a house with friends.

Jurors were also told Zadrozny was a landlord who did not pay tax on income from four of his properties, estimated in court to be "less than £15,000".

Zadrozny told the jury he did not keep the money for himself, and gave cash from the heritage society to Tony Brewer, a former Ashfield District Council chairman who died from Covid in 2020, to repair war memorials.

Zadrozny also helped set up a Classic Cinema Club for people who liked the Carry On films, which the court heard "was probably legitimate when he set it up" - although he later helped himself to its funds.

The court heard £5,000 was withdrawn in cash from the Ashfield Heritage Society account, while £1,200 was withdrawn from the cinema club.

Zadrozny denied the offences and told the trial the funds he had received were spent on the community.

The former council leader was found not guilty of three counts of fraud.

In mitigation, defence barrister Sam Robinson KC said up until 2015, Zadrozny was "a model citizen, in the way he has behaved in his public life but also in his personal life".

Robinson added: "He went off the rails from 2015 onwards. He blew his life spectacularly up.

"It's so easy to look at someone who has unravelled and think why on earth did he do any of this? That's the enigma we're dealing with."

He also said medical experts suggested mental health conditions could have caused "compromised judgement", and "can produce avoidance, indecision and impulsive behaviour".

However, in his sentencing remarks, the judge said Zadrozny had undertaken "dishonest conduct that took place over a number of years".

"I know that today is a shameful day for you," he said.

"When it became apparent that your offending would be uncovered, you sought to cover your tracks in an elaborate series of lies."

The judge said the sentence reflected the "gross abuse of trust", and how the "offending was conducted over a sustained period of time".

On 12 November, the district council confirmed that Zadrozny resigned as councillor for Larwood, adding there would be no by-election until the local elections in May.

The Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) also decided to launch a rapid review of the local authority after MPs raised concerns about a decision to appoint Zadrozny to the council's planning committee in the wake of his conviction.

Ten councillors quit the Ashfield Independents as a result, with some forming a new group called the District Alliance.

An MHCLG spokesperson added: "We have powers to investigate and intervene where councils fail to meet their Best Value Duty, and we're conducting a best-value assessment on Ashfield District Council to ensure it's delivering for local people."

In a letter to Labour MP Michelle Welsh, local government minister Jim McMahon confirmed he had ordered a "rapid best-value assessment" to be carried out into the authority.

Following the sentencing, Theresa Hodgkinson, chief executive at Ashfield District Council said Zadrozny "no longer has an affiliation with the council".

"We do understand why recent events may have damaged confidence in the council and caused concern across our communities," she said.

"Residents are right to expect the highest standards from those elected to represent them, and from their council, and while recent events cannot be changed, we are focused on rebuilding confidence in our council and maintaining and enhancing services and investment into the district.

"Our residents should be reassured that our focus remains firmly on providing high-quality services, investing in our communities and achieving the best outcomes for local people."

articles.title: When and where storms could slow your post-Thanksgiving travel
articles.summary: Another round of storms could slow the trip home from Thanksgiving for some across the country this weekend and into early next week.
articles.body: Another round of storms could slow the trip home from Thanksgiving for some across the country this weekend and into early next week. The messy weather ramps up Saturday and carries into Sunday, typically the busiest travel day of the year. The first storm will bring snow and strong winds to the Rockies Friday night before it spreads soaking rain across the Plains Saturday. But the real trouble is likely to set in Sunday morning as the storm intensifies, bringing potentially heavy rain and gusty winds from the Louisiana Gulf Coast to southern Michigan before reaching the Northeast by Sunday evening. A second storm will move into Pacific Northwest on Sunday and could impact travel along the West Coast as the work week starts. 🌧️ Track the storms in the CNN Weather app But we’re not expecting these weekend storms to pack the same punch as the system that hit the eastern United States on Thanksgiving. The sprawling storm stretched from Missouri to Massachusetts and set off major coasting flooding along the Mid-Atlantic while knocking out power to 900,000 customers at its peak on Thanksgiving Day. Wind gusts reached over 70 mph in the Northeast and forced the first postponement in the history of the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Water levels hit record highs along parts of the Mid-Atlantic coast, rising higher than they did during 2012’s Superstorm Sandy in a few spots. More than 500,000 homes and businesses were still without power as of Friday afternoon, according to PowerOutage.com. Light rain, snow showers and some winds up to 30 mph will linger across the Great Lakes, Ohio River Valley and Northeast through early Saturday before the holiday storm finally makes its exit. Here’s what to expect, by region, as the new storms move in this weekend: Pacific Northwest and Rockies Moderate rain is moving into Oregon and Washington Friday morning and will turn to mostly snow Friday night in Idaho, southern Montana and Wyoming. By Saturday morning, snow will push into northeastern Utah, Colorado and potentially into western Nebraska. Totals of 8 to 12 inches of snow are expected in the Rockies, with greater amounts possible in highest elevations. Winds gusting up to 50 mph or higher will accompany the snow in mountain areas and spread across portions of low-lying central Montana, southern Wyoming and eastern Colorado and into the central Plains. On Sunday, a second storm enters the Pacific Northwest, bringing heavy rain and wind to parts of California, Oregon and Washington. That system could help pull another strong storm into Southern California early next week. Central Plains The first storm moves out of the West and into the central Plains later on Saturday. Soaking rain will fall across Nebraska and expand into Kansas, southern Iowa and Missouri overnight through Sunday morning. Gusty winds from 40 to 60 mph will spread into western Kansas, northern Texas and Oklahoma overnight and could cause more power outages. Drivers heading home Saturday night should allow for extra time as wind and rain move in. Midwest, Gulf Coast and Southeast Travelers in and out of these regions face the greatest risk of disruptions on Sunday. Rain will move into Illinois by Sunday morning. As the storm swings east, a line of weak thunderstorms could form over the lower Mississippi Valley. Gusty wind and rain will spread across the broader Gulf Coast and Midwest during the day, tracking into the Southeast and Ohio River valley by Sunday evening. Widespread gusts between 20 to 30 mph and over a half inch of rain are expected. That timing lines up with the busiest travel day of the holiday period, when TSA expects more than 3 million people to go through checkpoints, which would be the most of any day so far this year. Northeast and Mid-Atlantic The storm arrives in the Mid-Atlantic and Northeast overnight Sunday. Soaking rain and gusty winds from 20 to 40 mph will continue from early Monday morning through midday, a window that could catch any late-night drivers and early Monday departures. Thanksgiving storm sets records, disrupts travel and power for thousands Thursday’s worst impacts were felt in the East. Power outages forced some families to have their Thanksgiving dinners by candlelight and outages are still affecting hundreds of thousands of customers on Friday. Pennsylvania and New Jersey have the most, with about 245,000 combined outages as of late Friday morning. In Maryland, 1.9 million people in Montgomery and Prince George’s counties were asked to limit water use after outages hit two water treatment plants, but the restriction was lifted early Friday. FlightAware counted 462 cancellations and more than 2,500 delays across the country Thursday. Wind damage also closed the Commodore Barry Bridge between Pennsylvania and New Jersey, which is expected to stay shut until at least Saturday. Strong winds shoved ocean water ashore on top of the already exceptional king tides, and gusts topped 60 mph in Maryland, Virginia, Delaware and North Carolina. At least 30 locations across Virginia, Maryland, Delaware and New Jersey experienced major flooding, with some locations reaching all-time highs and surpassing the level set during Superstorm Sandy by 1.5 feet or more. Records fell away from the coast, too. The storm dropped 8 to 12 inches of snow on a widespread swath of eastern Missouri and western Illinois, and St. Louis had its largest November snowstorm in 46 years. The weight of the snow brought down branches and power lines, pushing peak Missouri outages past 150,000 customers. Memphis saw snow on Thanksgiving for the first time in at least 70 years, and Nashville had its first Thanksgiving snowfall since 1950. In New York City, Central Park logged 1.82 inches of rain, making it the wettest Thanksgiving on record there.

articles.title: Mecca pact allies condemn ‘heinous’ Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia
articles.summary: Officials from Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye pledge to protect the kingdom’s security during talks in Islamabad.
articles.body:
Pakistan and Turkiye have renewed their pledge to support Saudi Arabia in safeguarding its security and sovereignty, as senior government and defence officials from the three countries denounced the continuing attacks by Yemen’s Houthis on the kingdom.

The statement followed a meeting of the Strategic Political and Defence Committee (SPDC) of the Mecca defence pact countries in the Pakistani capital, Islamabad, on Friday.

The three countries signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, under which an armed attack on one member is treated as an attack on all three. The committee comprises the three nations’ foreign and defence ministers alongside top military officials.

Pakistan’s Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar thanked the participating officials after the roughly two-and-a-half-hour meeting.

“The SPDC meeting reviewed the evolving regional security situation and reaffirmed the determination of the three countries to continue working collectively towards regional peace, security and stability,” he told reporters.

“The three sides reiterated their strong condemnation of the persistent and heinous attacks by the Houthi militia, targeting civilians and civilian infrastructure in the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia,” he said.

“They reaffirmed their collective resolve to continue and intensify efforts to support the kingdom in safeguarding its security, sovereignty, and territorial integrity, in accordance with the collective defence provisions of the Mecca Agreement for Joint Defence.”

The high-level talks come as Saudi Arabia continues to face attacks by the Iran-backed Houthis, who have repeatedly targeted Saudi cities, oil facilities and shipping since fighting in Yemen intensified in July.

At least 26 people have been killed in suspected Houthi drone and missile attacks in Saudi Arabia since September 23, according to Saudi authorities. Twenty-three of them were killed in strikes on airports.

These attacks were expected to top Friday’s agenda, but no details were released regarding any concrete measures.

At an emergency meeting of the pact’s members in Riyadh on October 5, the committee agreed to provide forces and capabilities and ensure their rapid deployment in the kingdom.

Pakistan has previously pledged to defend Saudi territory, while ruling out attacking the Houthis inside Yemen.

Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan also told Turkish media last week that Ankara’s current policy was aimed at the defence of Saudi Arabia.

“No decision has been made on deploying troops inside Yemen. However, the necessary support is being provided in defending Saudi Arabia,” he said.

Dar said Friday’s discussions also focused on implementing decisions made at previous meetings of the alliance, as well as boosting cooperation across various sectors.

“The parties reaffirmed their commitment to strengthening cooperation in defence industries, joint technological development, training, and capacity building, with a view to enhancing the collective capabilities and cohesion of their armed forces in order to address mutual security concerns and contribute to peace and security in the region,” he said.

Turkiye’s Fidan said that kind of integration sits at the core of the pact’s strategy.

“The greatest goal of this alliance is for countries here to pool their own capabilities – not only their military capabilities, but also their defence industry capabilities – to generate greater power, create greater impact, and make a larger contribution to peace and stability,” Anadolu news agency quoted him as saying after the meeting.

Fidan also said that ongoing negotiations between the US and Iran were discussed, while several decisions were made in principle regarding the roadmap to follow for other countries wishing to become members of the alliance.

Several regional nations have already expressed interest in joining the pact. In an August interview with Al Jazeera, Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan said Egypt could potentially join the pact.

Bangladesh has also stated it is actively considering joining the agreement, while Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said last month that Damascus is weighing whether to enter the Mecca alliance.

articles.title: Chicken Shop Date: The perfect end or a disappointing send-off?
articles.summary: Amelia Dimoldenberg has called time on her hit YouTube series Chicken Shop Date after more than a decade.
articles.body:
For better or worse, everyone recalls their first date. But how will the last one be remembered?

After more than a decade of serving up her awkward, off-the-wall questions, Amelia Dimoldenberg's Chicken Shop Date is no longer looking for love, with the YouTuber calling time on her hit series.

From a youth club project to a full-blown media empire with A-listers asking her out, the series has influenced the interview landscape and carved a new path for the next generation of content creators.

"To start my next chapter, I have to close this one," Dimoldenberg told the BBC earlier this month.

"I'm focussing on making sure I say goodbye in the perfect way so I feel ready to do my next thing."

After much speculation as to who would be the final date, fans were never going to be able to agree as to whether the farewell was indeed perfect.

Names like Harry Styles and Beyoncé had been floated around, but it was Drake who was the favourite with some bookies after Dimoldenberg previously described the Canadian rapper as her dream date.

So when the camera panned to psychotherapist Esther Perel, "everyone was a bit surprised", says fan Sarah Almond, who watched an early cinema screening on Tuesday.

"I wasn't familiar with Esther Perel myself and I don't think anyone else in the cinema was aware of who she was," the content creator tells BBC Newsbeat.

And when the episode went live on YouTube, while most viewers reacted positively to the choice of guest, some said they did not recognise her and asked "where's Drake?!".

"I did hear a few people say they were disappointed, but I wasn't disappointed at all," Almond says.

"Even though I was expecting a bigger name to go off with a big bang, it was exactly what the show needed."

The episode played out like a counselling session, becoming emotional at points, Almond says.

"She's treating the end of Chicken Shop Date like it's a relationship break-up.

"It served her really well. It was a nice goodbye."

Signing off with an interview with a relationships expert is a sign of the journey Dimoldenberg has been on with her pioneering series.

With more than three million YouTube subscribers, Chicken Shop Date has climbed the pecking order to become a key stop on press tours for even some of the world's biggest names, including the likes of Cher and Sir Paul McCartney.

Rachel Adeolu watched the series from the very beginning, when Dimoldenberg would mostly date emerging rap and grime artists.

"A chicken shop is somewhere that's very familiar to a lot of people who grew up in London," the 21-year-old says. "It's kind of like a third space where a lot of us built friendships.

"So seeing content creators who also looked like us being interviewed in that same kind of setting with this unconventional interview style, which was also very funny, was unheard of."

By 2021, seven years on from the first episode, the show was starting to look different.

As well as rappers and content creators, Dimoldenberg was bagging interviews with pop stars like Ed Sheeran and Finneas, as well as footballers Tammy Abraham and John Stones.

It was about that time producer Liv West joined the team, and her background at a major music publisher helped the series secure an impressive roster of guests.

"That summer we had a really big line-up," she says, with the likes of Keke Palmer, Charli XCX and Rosalía looking for love at first bite.

"It was then we started to think the tides are changing," she adds.

As the profiles of the dates grew though, so did their teams, with West saying it became a challenge to squeeze everyone in for shoots - with some being put into the kitchen.

The producer feels things ramped up after the episode with documentary maker Louis Theroux, as he was not a typical guest and of "legendary status".

For earlier fans like Adeolu, the take-off came at a cost.

"It feels like the audience who are more interested in seeing A-list celebrities be interviewed, they have definitely been favoured over the people who made the show popular in the first place," she says.

"In terms of just the initial charm of what the show was, I think that has probably had a negative impact on it."

As Dimoldenberg reached new audiences, her success started to balloon and before long she was appearing on major red carpets, in films and magazines - as well as a guest on other people's talk shows.

It also allowed her to work on a passion project: Dimz Inc Academy.

Launched in 2025, the scheme aims to upskill and mentor young people from underrepresented backgrounds who want to get into creative industries.

"It was Amelia's big dream to really make the creative industry, and particularly digital entertainment, accessible from every walk of life for every young person," West says.

Now in its second year, the scheme will be a legacy for the series away from screens - but as for what's next for the series' star, that's yet to be revealed.

"I really want to spend more time writing, that's what I'd like to focus on in the future," Dimoldenberg told the BBC.

"But who knows, the possibilities are endless."

Additional reporting by Naomi Clarke, Miya Chahal and Srosh Khan.
